Yodel Scam Text Messages: How to Spot a Fake Yodel Text (UK)

A text from 'Yodel' says your parcel needs a small fee or new details? Yodel now runs as Yodel by InPost, and tracking has moved — here is how to check a delivery properly and spot the fake.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-06-05 · Updated 2026-08-10 · 7 min read

Quick answer: Yodel by InPost says it never asks for a redelivery fee or for your bank details by text, so a text demanding one is a scam. Genuine import charges arise elsewhere in a purchase, not by redelivery text. Yodel web accounts ended on 17 July 2026: check parcels in the InPost app or at inpost.co.uk, opened yourself.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What changed in July 2026, and why scammers benefit

Yodel now operates as Yodel by InPost, and the customer-facing tools moved during July 2026. Yodel's own help centre says the Yodel by InPost app is no longer available from 17 July, and InPost's Yodel help page says Yodel by InPost web accounts also stopped being available from that date. Parcels are handled by InPost, and customers are told to use the InPost app or inpost.co.uk to track and manage deliveries.

That transition is exactly the kind of moment smishing gangs wait for. When people are unsure which app, brand, or web address is now correct, a text saying "your Yodel parcel needs attention" is harder to dismiss. InPost also warns that during the move you may receive updates from both Yodel by InPost and InPost, so two genuine senders is now normal — which removes the easy assumption that anything unexpected must be fake.

The practical rule has not changed, though: judge a delivery message by whether you can match it to a real parcel through a route you opened yourself, never by the branding or the link inside it.

What a fake Yodel text is trying to get

A Yodel scam text impersonates the courier so you tap a link and hand over payment or personal details. It usually claims a delivery failed, a parcel is waiting, or an address needs confirming, then asks for a small 'redelivery' or 'release' fee.

These are sent in bulk to random numbers. The sender has no idea whether you have ordered anything — the bet is simply that many people have a parcel moving at any given time. The small fee is deliberate: a couple of pounds feels too trivial to be worth defrauding someone over, which is what makes people enter a card number. The card details are the actual target, and a follow-up call impersonating your bank is where the large losses happen.

The one commitment that settles a fee demand

Yodel by InPost's own fraud and information-security page states it will never send emails or text messages asking you to provide your bank details or phone number, and that it will never ask for a fee for redelivery of a parcel.

So a message demanding money to release or redeliver a parcel contradicts the courier's own published commitment, whichever brand name it uses. Note the limit of that rule: it covers redelivery fees and requests for bank details or phone numbers. Genuine delivery notifications do exist, and a retailer or an import charge can legitimately involve money elsewhere in a purchase — so "a message mentioned money" is not the test. "A courier asked me to pay a fee to get my parcel redelivered" is.

Signs the text is not from the courier

  • It asks for any payment to receive or redeliver a parcel.
  • It asks for bank details, card details, or your phone number.
  • The link is not on inpost.co.uk or yodel.co.uk — watch for added words, hyphens, or unusual endings.
  • It arrives from a random mobile or international number.
  • It pressures you with a deadline, a holding fee, or a threat to return the parcel.
  • You cannot match it to an order you actually placed.
  • It asks for a one-time passcode, password, or date of birth. Yodel's fraud page notes that genuine companies do not email asking for usernames, passwords, dates of birth, or card details. These waves cluster around bank holidays, when a missed delivery is most believable; our bank holiday parcel scam guide covers the timing.

Checking a delivery now that tracking has moved

Do not tap the link in the message. Instead:

  • Find the tracking number in the dispatch confirmation from the shop you ordered from, not from the text.
  • Open the InPost app, or type inpost.co.uk into your browser yourself, and enter that tracking number.
  • If you still have a Yodel tracking reference, yodel.co.uk remains the brand's own site and directs customers to the current InPost route — reach it by typing the address, never through a message link.
  • Ask the retailer which courier is carrying the order and whether anything is genuinely out for delivery. The retailer is often the fastest independent check.

A genuine tracking page shows your parcel without asking for a card number, a PIN, a banking password, or a one-time passcode. Yodel's fraud page also says its legitimate emails come from donotreply@yodel.co.uk or noreply@yodel.co.uk, which is useful context for email — but treat a sender address as a clue, not proof, because sender details can be spoofed.

If you tapped the link or entered details

Delivery scams have a distinctive second act, so the order of these steps matters.

  • Call your bank on the number printed on your card and say you may have entered card details on a fake courier site. Ask them to stop the card and watch the account.
  • Expect a follow-up. Criminals who harvest details from a parcel page often ring within days posing as your bank's fraud team, using the real details you just gave them to sound credible. No genuine bank will tell you to move money to a safe account. Hang up and call back on the number on your card.
  • Treat any one-time passcode you shared as compromised, and change any password you typed.
  • Keep the message and any payment receipt before deleting anything — you will need them to report.

If money has left your account, the payment route decides what protection applies. Our scam recovery checklist sets out the card, transfer, account and identity steps in order, including how reporting differs in Scotland.

Reporting a fake Yodel or InPost text

Forward the text free to 7726. That shortcode is run by the mobile networks and lets them investigate and block the sender.

Yodel's fraud page asks customers to forward suspicious emails to information.security@yodel.co.uk rather than clicking anything inside them, so the brand can act on fake domains. Phishing emails can also go to the National Cyber Security Centre at report@phishing.gov.uk.

If you lost money or handed over details, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Yodel app still available?

No. Yodel's help centre says the Yodel by InPost app is no longer available from 17 July, and InPost says Yodel by InPost web accounts stopped being available from the same date. Parcels are handled by InPost, so tracking and delivery preferences now live in the InPost app or at inpost.co.uk. Reach either by typing the address yourself rather than following a link in a message.

Does Yodel charge a fee to redeliver a parcel?

No. Yodel by InPost's fraud page says it will never ask for a fee for redelivery of a parcel, and will never email or text asking for your bank details or phone number. A message demanding a small 'redelivery' or 'release' fee through a link is a scam aimed at your card details.

A text still says 'Yodel' — does the rebrand make it fake?

Not by itself. Yodel by InPost is a live brand and you may receive genuine updates from both Yodel by InPost and InPost while the move completes, so Yodel branding alone proves nothing either way. Check whether the message matches a real order by entering the tracking number from your dispatch confirmation into the InPost app or inpost.co.uk, opened independently.

I entered my card details on a courier link — what now?

Ring your bank on the number on your card, say you entered details on a fake courier site, and ask them to stop the card and monitor the account. Change anything else you typed, and treat a shared one-time passcode as compromised. Be ready for a call claiming to be the bank's fraud team — that is the next stage of the same scam. Then work through the scam recovery checklist.

Where do I report a fake courier text?

Forward it free to 7726 so your network can act on the sender. Suspicious emails can go to Yodel at information.security@yodel.co.uk and to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk. If money or details were lost, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

Fast checks

  • Pause before sending money or credentials
  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
